rhs_question_text: A wildlife-rescue centre needs to order animal weights from smallest to largest using bubble sort. Describe a complete bubble-sort procedure that would work for an array of weights, including how comparisons, swaps and repeated passes are handled. [5]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Set a Boolean swap flag or similar. Compare each adjacent pair. If already ordered, leave the pair unchanged; if out of order, exchange them (a temporary variable is one option) and record that a swap happened. Repeat adjacent comparisons across the array and perform further passes until no swaps occur or the maximum number of passes has been reached.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Five marks for five distinct accurate stages from: flag/condition; adjacent comparison; no swap for ordered pair; swap disordered pair; exchange using temporary storage; update flag; finish full pass; repeat passes until ordered. The explanation of multiple passes must be clear.

rhs_question_text: The same rescue centre improves its bubble sort by recording whether a swap happened in each pass. Explain how this can allow the algorithm to stop early, rather than always performing its maximum number of passes. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Reset the Boolean swap flag at the start of each pass. Set it when any two items are exchanged; if the pass finishes with the flag still false, there were no swaps so all items are in order and further passes stop.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for tracking whether swaps occurred, one for stopping when the most recent complete pass had no swaps. A reference to the flag or equivalent condition is required.

rhs_question_text: An ecology class records four sample masses in the following order: 20, 8, 15, 36. Describe how insertion sort builds an ascending sorted list from these four values, showing the sorted and unsorted portions after each insertion. [5]

rhs_marking_rule_draft: Up to five marks: identify the sorted/unsorted partitions and show the four insertions correctly, using these exact four values. Generic statements alone cannot earn the application marks.

rhs_question_text:
A wildlife-rescue centre has an array of animal record identifiers and uses the following original pseudocode to sort them into ascending order:

01 function split(values, low, high)
02   pivot = values[high]
03   boundary = low
04   for index = low to high - 1
05     if values[index] < pivot then
06       temp = values[boundary]
07       values[boundary] = values[index]
08       values[index] = temp
09       boundary = boundary + 1
10     endif
11   next index
12   temp = values[boundary]
13   values[boundary] = values[high]
14   values[high] = temp
15   return boundary
16 endfunction
17 procedure quickSort(values, low, high)
18   if low < high then
19     position = split(values, low, high)
20     quickSort(values, low, position - 1)
21     quickSort(values, position + 1, high)
22   endif
23 endprocedure

Name the recursive routine, then identify the two numbered lines on which that routine calls itself. [2]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Recursive routine: quickSort. Recursive call lines: 20 and 21.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: One mark for naming quickSort; one for identifying both call locations, lines 20 AND 21. The new line numbers apply to RHS-authored code, not the OCR source listing.

rhs_question_text:
A public library holds 500,000 book records, sorted by their numeric catalogue ID. Staff frequently need to find one record by ID. They are considering linear search and binary search.

Use this comparison data:
Method | Worst-case time | Average-case time | Auxiliary space
Linear | O(n) | O(n) | O(1)
Binary | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(1)

Evaluate the two approaches for this particular library. Explain how each method works, interpret the complexity data for a large sorted collection, and justify your recommendation. [9]
rhs_answer_points_draft: Linear search checks records sequentially and can examine many entries; binary search compares the middle ID and discards half the remaining range after each comparison, requiring sorted data. With 500,000 already-sorted records, logarithmic searching is much more efficient in average and worst-case comparisons while both methods require constant auxiliary space in iterative form. Choose binary search for repeated exact-ID lookups; explain why linear may still be simpler or suitable for unsorted data or very small inputs.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Teacher-marked nine-mark response: 7–9 detailed, balanced explanation applied to 500,000 sorted records and justified choice; 4–6 sound but incomplete application; 1–3 basic knowledge with limited evaluation; 0 no credit. rhs_answer_points_draft: Data mining analyses large volumes of data, derives useful information from them, and identifies patterns, trends, anomalies or relationships not immediately obvious.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Three separate marks for large-scale analysis; making data useful; identifying hidden patterns/trends/relationships/anomalies.

rhs_question_text:
An environmental-monitoring computer processes four instructions I1, I2, I3 and I4. Each instruction has three stages: Fetch (F), Decode (D) and Execute (E). A sequential processor completes F, D and E on I1 before beginning I2. A pipelined processor can carry out different stages of different instructions during the same clock cycle.

Assume each stage takes exactly one cycle and there are no dependencies or stalls. Explain and evaluate pipelining for these four instructions using a labelled cycle-by-cycle example. Consider the difference between throughput and the time needed for an individual instruction, and one situation that reduces pipeline efficiency. [9]
rhs_answer_points_draft:
Ideal pipeline by cycle:
1: F1
2: D1 and F2
3: E1, D2 and F3
4: E2, D3 and F4
5: E3 and D4
6: E4
Sequential execution takes 12 stage-cycles for four instructions, while ideal three-stage pipelining completes the group in 6 cycles. Pipelining overlaps work to increase throughput; each instruction still needs to pass through three stages, so latency is not necessarily reduced. Branches/jumps, dependencies or pipeline flushes create stalls and reduce the theoretical gain.
rhs_marking_rule_draft: Holistic 9 marks: 7–9 thorough, correct staged example with a balanced throughput/dependency evaluation; 4–6 sound but underdeveloped; 1–3 basic; 0 nothing creditworthy. Award teacher-marked levels of response rather than a 9-keyword count.

rhs_answer_points_draft: Object-based lists may grow or shrink dynamically and encapsulate behaviour in reusable classes, but node allocation and references add overhead and searching typically follows pointers sequentially. A fixed-capacity 2D array can be compact/predictable and indexable directly by physical slot but needs spare capacity, a free-list or occupancy scheme and careful pointer-index maintenance; it may waste unused slots or reach capacity. Neither representation permits constant-time search for an arbitrary value simply by being a linked structure. A strong answer applies these trade-offs to volatile sighting volumes and defends a choice, including circumstances where a bounded-size array could still be sensible.
